label: General background, not the authors' interpretation

statements.title: Making a soluble cadmium feed
statements.summary: A carboxylic acid such as oleic acid can convert cadmium oxide into cadmium carboxylate in the flask. Changing this soluble feed and the free acid changes cadmium availability during nucleation and growth.

statements.title: Oleate and the nanocrystal surface
statements.summary: Bound oleate can stabilize dispersed metal chalcogenide nanocrystals, and not all surface carboxylate need occupy the same binding environment. Displacing metal carboxylate from the surface can change surface stoichiometry as well as colloidal stability.

statements.title: Octadecene is not always inert
statements.summary: Octadecene provides a weakly coordinating medium for hot solution growth, leaving the ligands more freedom to control surface binding. It can also polymerize under growth conditions, leaving an alkene-derived residue that is difficult to separate from hydrophobic nanocrystals.

statements.title: Aqueous thiol-capped growth
statements.summary: In aqueous cadmium chalcogenide synthesis, a thiol with a water-compatible group can stabilize growing particles in the liquid. Solution acidity changes thiol speciation, so the precursor equilibria and the resulting surface coverage can change together.

statements.title: Oleylamine can act as both solvent and reductant
statements.summary: In amine-mediated noble-metal syntheses, oleylamine can help reduce the metal precursor while also binding the particle surface. Reduction and adsorption therefore affect both the formation of nuclei and the persistence of exposed facets.

statements.title: A primary amine can change surface growth
statements.summary: Oleylamine can coordinate soluble metal species and bind exposed surface sites during colloidal growth. It can therefore change how rapidly precursors react and how readily the resulting particles remain dispersed.

statements.title: Precipitation can select particles by size
statements.summary: When ethanol is used as a poor solvent for ligand-coated nanocrystals, it can precipitate part of the dispersion without a new solid-forming reaction. Choosing how far precipitation proceeds can separate size fractions as well as remove soluble residues.

statements.title: Methanol and ligand-coated particles
statements.summary: In a size-selective precipitation, methanol can reduce the dispersing power of a nonpolar solvent for particles bearing hydrocarbon ligands. Which fraction precipitates depends on particle size and the surface coating, as well as the solvent mixture.

statements.title: Antisolvent washing
statements.summary: When acetone serves as an antisolvent for hydrophobically capped particles, it can move the crystals into a precipitate while some free ligand remains in solution. Repeated precipitation and redispersion can change the amount of loosely associated material left at the surface.

statements.title: A phosphine can carry a chalcogen feed
statements.summary: Trioctylphosphine can solubilize elemental selenium or tellurium as a phosphine chalcogenide for colloidal growth. Delivering the chalcogen in this bonded form changes the chemistry that supplies reactive growth species.

statements.title: Selenium delivery from TOP–Se
statements.summary: Trioctylphosphine selenide carries selenium in a soluble feed, rather than as separate solid selenium. The conversion of that feed can affect how much selenium is available while nuclei form and grow.

statements.title: Preparing a selenium feed in phosphine
statements.summary: Elemental selenium and trioctylphosphine can form a soluble selenium feed before injection. Preforming that feed separates selenium dissolution from the event that starts nanocrystal nucleation.

statements.title: TOPO as a coordinating medium
statements.summary: Trioctylphosphine oxide supplies a coordinating medium in which metal chalcogenide nanocrystals can nucleate and grow. Coordination at the particle surface influences which growth sites remain accessible and how the particles disperse afterward.

statements.title: Cadmium oxide needs conversion to a soluble feed
statements.summary: Cadmium oxide is a solid precursor that can be converted into a soluble cadmium complex by an acidic ligand. That conversion makes it possible to control the cadmium delivered during nucleation without using a volatile organocadmium feed.

statements.title: A reactive organocadmium feed
statements.summary: Dimethylcadmium can supply cadmium directly in a hot-injection route instead of requiring an oxide to dissolve and form a complex first. Its different activation chemistry can change how quickly the mixture becomes supersaturated and nucleates.

statements.title: Cadmium phosphonates and elongated growth
statements.summary: Phosphonic acids can coordinate cadmium and alter the relative growth rates of the surfaces of wurtzite cadmium selenide. When the growth supply sustains that difference, elongation can compete with more uniform growth.

statements.title: A phosphonate can bias shape evolution
statements.summary: Long-chain phosphonic acids can modify both cadmium availability and surface chemistry in wurtzite cadmium selenide growth. Changes in those processes can favor axial growth over growth across the rod.

statements.title: Water-compatible thiolate capping
statements.summary: In aqueous cadmium chalcogenide growth, a mercaptocarboxylic acid can bind surface cadmium through sulfur while its carboxylate promotes water dispersibility. Changes in acidity alter the balance between metal complexation, surface binding, and dispersion.

statements.title: Aqueous cadmium and thiol complexation
statements.summary: A thiolate can coordinate cadmium from a water-soluble salt such as cadmium chloride before the chalcogenide forms. Soluble complexation and surface passivation both depend on thiol speciation, so the two effects cannot always be tuned independently.

statements.title: Citrate participates in gold nucleation
statements.summary: In citrate reduction, citrate participates in the reduction of dissolved gold and can help stabilize the resulting dispersion. Changing the conditions for reduction changes how gold is divided between new nuclei and growing particles.

statements.title: Citrate reduction of a dissolved gold salt
statements.summary: In the citrate route, a dissolved gold chloride precursor supplies metal while citrate participates in reduction and dispersion. The balance between nucleation and growth influences the resulting particle size distribution.

statements.title: Dodecanethiol supplies the gold surface coating
statements.summary: In a two-phase gold synthesis, an alkanethiol binds the new gold surface through sulfur. Its hydrocarbon tail helps the particles disperse in the organic phase and limits aggregation during isolation.

statements.title: A strong reductant starts gold nucleation
statements.summary: Borohydride can turn a soluble gold precursor into gold rapidly in a two-phase thiol route. Formation of new nuclei competes with growth on existing particles, while the surface ligand helps limit coalescence.

statements.title: Toluene as the organic phase
statements.summary: Toluene provides an organic phase for the transferred gold precursor and for the thiol-coated particles in the two-phase route. Phase transfer and ligand binding allow precursor conversion and product dispersion to occur in different chemical environments from the initial salt solution.

statements.title: Silver and bromide surfactant in gold-rod growth
statements.summary: A silver additive and a bromide-bearing surfactant can modify axial relative to lateral growth in seed-mediated gold synthesis. Their effects are coupled to the growth solution and surface environment rather than being independent shape controls.

statements.title: Surfactant-mediated gold growth
statements.summary: Cetyltrimethylammonium bromide helps define the surface and ionic environment around gold seeds during rod growth. The resulting difference between axial and lateral growth depends on the rest of the growth solution as well as the surfactant.

statements.title: A reactive sulfur feed
statements.summary: Bis(trimethylsilyl)sulfide can supply sulfur rapidly to a reactive metal precursor in a nonaqueous colloidal route. The resulting rate of sulfur delivery affects the period over which new nuclei can form.

statements.title: A reactive phosphide feed changes growth timing
statements.summary: Tris(trimethylsilyl)phosphine reacts with indium carboxylate in common colloidal indium phosphide routes. Rapid precursor conversion does not necessarily make all particles form at once, because molecular clusters can participate before continued crystal growth.

statements.title: Indium carboxylate as a precursor
statements.summary: Indium acetate can be exchanged into a more soluble indium carboxylate by a long-chain acid before a phosphorus reagent is added. Conversion of the carboxylate and the formation of intermediate clusters can separate precursor consumption from the emergence of larger crystals.

statements.title: A polyol can act as solvent and reductant
statements.summary: Ethylene glycol can dissolve metal precursors and participate in reduction in a polyol synthesis. The rate of reduction relative to surface stabilization influences nucleation and growth.

statements.title: Nucleation and size focusing
statements.summary: A rapid change in precursor availability can create a short nucleation period followed by growth on existing particles. Growth can narrow the size distribution while material is supplied, whereas later ripening can consume smaller particles and change that distribution again.

statements.title: Alternate supply during shell growth
statements.summary: Sequential cation and anion additions can favor growth at existing nanocrystal surfaces rather than the formation of separate particles. Core and shell lattice mismatch can build strain at the interface as the shell develops.

statements.title: Cations can be replaced within a particle
statements.summary: Cation exchange can replace one set of cations while substantially retaining the anion framework of an ionic nanocrystal. The extent and location of exchange depend on ion mobility and the relative stability of the phases, so partial exchange can give distinct material domains.

statements.title: Stable cluster intermediates can delay particle growth
statements.summary: In some indium phosphide routes, unusually stable molecular clusters accumulate instead of turning immediately into a smoothly growing distribution. Their appearance breaks the simple link between mixing the precursor and forming the final nanocrystals.

statements.title: Lead oleate can form in the flask
statements.summary: Oleic acid can convert lead oxide to a soluble lead carboxylate in colloidal lead sulfide synthesis. That step affects how lead is supplied to the growth solution and also leaves carboxylate available to stabilize the particle surface.

statements.title: Long-chain ligands can replace acetate
statements.summary: A long-chain acid such as oleic acid can exchange with acetate at the zinc precursor in liquid-phase growth. Changing the carboxylate can alter precursor solubility and surface binding, which changes how growth proceeds.

statements.title: An indium carboxylate feed
statements.summary: Oleic acid can exchange with acetate when preparing an indium carboxylate feed for colloidal phosphide growth. The carboxylate environment affects how molecular intermediates and particle surfaces accommodate indium.

statements.title: Dissolved sulfide supplies sulfur for precipitation
statements.summary: Sodium sulfide supplies dissolved sulfide species for low-solubility metal sulfides in aqueous synthesis. Changing acidity changes sulfide speciation and can shift when precipitation overtakes complexation.

statements.title: Thiourea can release sulfide in the bath
statements.summary: Thiourea is a sulfur-bearing precursor that can generate reactive sulfur species as the solution chemistry proceeds. Sulfur delivery coupled to precursor conversion can change the balance between surface growth and unwanted precipitation in the bulk.

statements.title: Ammonia moderates free metal in a bath
statements.summary: Ammonia can complex dissolved metal ions in a chemical bath, keeping some metal out of the free-ion pool. The competition between complexation and precipitation affects whether growth occurs mainly on the intended surface or throughout the liquid.

statements.title: Base changes thiol speciation
statements.summary: Changing the acidity of an aqueous thiol-capped synthesis changes the amount of thiolate available to coordinate the metal or bind the crystal surface. It can therefore alter precipitation as well as the stability of the final dispersion.

statements.title: Acid can change capping-ligand binding
statements.summary: When used for acidity adjustment in an aqueous thiol-capped synthesis, acid changes the equilibrium between thiol and thiolate. Ligand protonation can change dissolved metal complexation and the colloidal stability of ligand-coated crystals.

statements.title: An inert atmosphere limits oxygen exposure
statements.summary: A nitrogen blanket can limit oxygen exposure during hot solution synthesis when an air-sensitive feed or surface is present. It helps preserve the intended precursor and surface chemistry without being a source of the nanocrystal elements.

statements.title: Excluding air during colloidal growth
statements.summary: An argon atmosphere can limit contact between air and reactive precursors during hot colloidal growth. Protecting the feed from oxidation helps keep the supply of growth species distinct from side reactions with air.

statements.title: A nonpolar liquid disperses hydrocarbon-capped particles
statements.summary: Hexane can redisperse nanocrystals whose surface ligands present hydrocarbon groups to the liquid. Its compatibility with the capping layer contrasts with the poor-solvent conditions used to precipitate that same dispersion.

statements.title: Solvent choice follows the surface coating
statements.summary: Chloroform can disperse many nanocrystals coated with organic ligands after colloidal growth. This dispersibility reflects the particle surface and does not establish that the crystalline core dissolved.

statements.title: Saturated carboxylic acids can supply coordinating carboxylate
statements.summary: Stearic acid can make a long-chain metal carboxylate when it reacts with a metal oxide or exchanges with a shorter ligand. Both the identity of the soluble feed and carboxylate binding at the surface can affect colloidal growth.

statements.title: Myristate binds indium and particle surfaces
statements.summary: In colloidal indium phosphide synthesis, myristic acid can supply a carboxylate for soluble indium species and a stabilizing ligand for the growing solid. Carboxylate coordination can help determine which molecular intermediates persist during growth.

statements.title: An alkylamine changes the ligand environment
statements.summary: Hexadecylamine can supplement other ligands in hot solution growth by coordinating accessible surface metal sites. A later ligand exchange can change surface passivation even if the underlying crystal remains the same.

statements.title: Alkylamine coordination and exchange
statements.summary: Dodecylamine can bind surface metal sites in colloidal cadmium chalcogenide syntheses. Replacing a labile amine with a more strongly binding ligand changes surface chemistry and can change how the particles disperse.

statements.title: A short donor ligand can replace a growth ligand
statements.summary: When pyridine is used for post-growth ligand exchange, its nitrogen donor can interact with exposed metal sites after bulky growth ligands are displaced. A shorter coating changes particle interactions and can alter the liquids that disperse the particles.

statements.title: An organozinc feed is chemically distinct from a zinc salt
statements.summary: Diethylzinc supplies zinc in a reactive organometallic form in some shell growth routes. Its conversion chemistry differs from a zinc carboxylate or oxide, so changing feeds can shift the balance between shell deposition and separate nucleation.

statements.title: A zinc carboxylate carries zinc into a nonpolar phase
statements.summary: Zinc stearate provides a zinc species compatible with a hydrophobic growth medium. Conversion of that feed and its binding environment can influence whether zinc reaches existing surfaces or contributes to other growth.

statements.title: Titanium alkoxide hydrolysis starts network formation
statements.summary: Titanium isopropoxide can hydrolyze and then condense to form titanium–oxygen connectivity in a sol-gel route. How hydrolysis and condensation compete affects the structure of the early oxide network.

statements.title: Urea can provide gradual basification
statements.summary: Under aqueous heating, urea can generate basic species as it decomposes. Gradual basification changes the buildup of supersaturation, which can affect how uniformly a metal hydroxide or oxide precursor precipitates.

statements.title: A thiol can affect both precursor and surface
statements.summary: A water-compatible thiol can bind precursor metal in solution and the metal-rich sites on a growing chalcogenide surface. Because these processes share the same ligand, acidity can jointly affect the growth rate and the coating that remains on the nanocrystal.

statements.title: A long-chain primary amine coordinates metal sites
statements.summary: During amine-assisted colloidal growth, octadecylamine can coordinate surface metal sites while keeping the surface compatible with a nonpolar liquid. Changing the capping layer changes which sites remain available for growth.

statements.title: A phosphonic acid can change cadmium selenide shape evolution
statements.summary: Hexylphosphonic acid can act as a coordinating ligand in cadmium selenide growth. Cadmium binding in solution and differences in surface growth rates can change which crystal dimensions grow fastest.

statements.title: A thiol end and a water-compatible end
statements.summary: Thioglycolic acid can bind to cadmium chalcogenide surfaces through sulfur while its carboxylate interacts with water. Acid–base speciation changes how the ligand partitions between precursor complexes and growing surfaces.

statements.title: Thioglycerol can keep particles dispersed in water
statements.summary: In aqueous cadmium chalcogenide growth, thioglycerol can bind surface cadmium through sulfur while the hydroxyl groups remain accessible to water. That capping layer influences the stability of the dispersion and the surface sites available for growth.

statements.title: A sulfur donor whose reactivity depends on the liquid
statements.summary: Thioacetamide can produce sulfide species during heated solution growth, rather than supplying the full reactive sulfide dose immediately. Its conversion can therefore affect the competition between separate nucleation and growth at existing surfaces.

statements.title: Alkalinity changes dissolved growth species
statements.summary: Sodium hydroxide can change which soluble hydroxide complexes exist during hydrothermal growth. That shifts the balance between dissolution and precipitation and can change the phase that crystallizes.

statements.title: A hydrated acetate can supply soluble zinc
statements.summary: Zinc acetate dihydrate can supply a zinc precursor in a liquid oxide synthesis. Hydrolysis and condensation of the dissolved species participate in forming the zinc–oxygen network rather than simply copying the structure of the starting salt.

statements.title: An acetate salt must enter a soluble growth feed
statements.summary: Cadmium acetate used in nonaqueous colloidal growth can exchange ligands with the surrounding carboxylic acids. The resulting ligand environment changes the availability of cadmium for precipitation or growth on existing crystals.

statements.title: Aminoarsine conversion depends on reduction
statements.summary: An aminoarsine provides an alternative arsenic feed in colloidal indium arsenide synthesis. Its transformation depends on the reductant environment, which can change how quickly arsenic becomes available to nucleating and growing nanocrystals.

statements.title: Aminophosphine supplies phosphorus through a different pathway
statements.summary: In aminophosphine-based indium phosphide synthesis, ligand exchange and phosphorus conversion can occur before the particles grow. This changes the relation between precursor consumption, nucleation, and the supply of phosphorus to existing particles.

statements.title: An amino-substituted phosphorus precursor must first react
statements.summary: Tris(diethylamino)phosphine is an amino-substituted phosphorus source rather than a preformed metal phosphide. Its precursor chemistry affects how rapidly phosphorus becomes available to the indium feed and growing crystals.

statements.title: Coordinating solvent helps dissolve lead halide
statements.summary: Trioctylphosphine oxide can help solubilize lead halide through metal–oxygen coordination in halide nanocrystal synthesis. Changing how the halide feed is dissolved influences the supply of species that form the crystalline product.

statements.title: Sequencing shell precursors separates growth events
statements.summary: Sequential cation and anion supply can bias crystallization toward an existing particle rather than promoting independent nucleation from a premixed solution. The result depends on how growth species reach the existing interface.

statements.title: Indium chloride supplies indium in aminophosphine synthesis
statements.summary: Indium chloride supplies indium to a solution whose amines and aminophosphine can coordinate the metal before indium phosphide forms. That precursor environment affects conversion and is distinct from the conversion of a preformed silyl phosphide feed.

statements.title: Zinc halide changes the coordination environment
statements.summary: A zinc halide additive can participate in the coordination chemistry of aminophosphine-based indium phosphide growth without being the phosphorus source. That environment can change the growth and surface chemistry of the resulting nanocrystals.

statements.title: A long-chain carboxylate carries cadmium in solution
statements.summary: Cadmium oleate provides a soluble cadmium feed in nonpolar nanocrystal growth. This couples metal availability to carboxylate chemistry rather than requiring solid cadmium oxide to dissolve during nucleation.

statements.title: Acetate can be exchanged before colloidal growth
statements.summary: Cadmium acetate can exchange with a long-chain carboxylic acid to make a feed better suited to a nonpolar liquid. That precursor conversion can change when the mixture supplies cadmium to nuclei and existing crystals.

statements.title: Oleic acid helps put cesium into a soluble feed
statements.summary: Oleic acid can convert cesium carbonate into cesium oleate for hot solution synthesis of cesium lead halide nanocrystals. Preparing that feed separately helps control when cesium becomes available to form the crystalline phase.

statements.title: Cysteine can bind by sulfur and disperse in water
statements.summary: The sulfur group of cysteine can bind surface metal sites as an aqueous chalcogenide nanocrystal forms. Its other functional groups interact with the liquid, linking surface coordination to dispersion stability.

statements.title: A diamine can activate elemental sulfur in solution
statements.summary: A sulfur–ethylenediamine feed can bring elemental sulfur into a reactive solution for sulfur nanocrystal formation. The amine environment changes how sulfur is delivered to the growing material rather than acting only as an inert liquid.

statements.title: A hydrophilic thiol can cap hydrothermal dots
statements.summary: In aqueous hydrothermal cadmium telluride growth, an acetylated cysteine ligand can bind surface cadmium through sulfur. Its water-compatible groups help stabilize the dispersed particles after growth.

statements.title: Ligand exchange can alter surface stoichiometry
statements.summary: A neutral donor is an L-type ligand, an anionic ligand can be X-type, and a surface-bound Lewis acid can act as Z-type. Displacing a Lewis-acidic metal carboxylate during ligand exchange can change surface stoichiometry as well as the coating.

statements.title: Technical-grade TOPO is not always chemically equivalent to purified TOPO
statements.summary: Phosphorus-containing impurities in technical-grade TOPO can change cadmium precursor coordination and surface binding during colloidal growth. They can therefore change shape selection without a change in the nominal solvent name.

statements.title: Oleylamine changes how sulfur is delivered
statements.summary: An amine can convert elemental sulfur into soluble polysulfide species before metal sulfide nanocrystals form. How sulfur is made available from that solution affects whether new nuclei form or existing particles keep growing.

statements.title: Strain and growth interruptions affect epitaxial islands
statements.summary: In strain-driven indium arsenide epitaxy, a wetting layer can give way to islands as the growing film relieves lattice strain. During a growth interruption the surface can continue to reorganize, so the island population need not remain fixed when the incoming flux changes.

statements.title: A phosphine sulfide feed changes sulfur conversion
statements.summary: Trioctylphosphine sulfide provides sulfur in a soluble, coordinated feed for chalcogenide growth. Differences in precursor conversion can affect whether sulfur is incorporated at an existing surface or helps form a separate phase.

statements.title: Phosphine identity changes selenium delivery
statements.summary: Tributylphosphine selenide is a molecular selenium source in colloidal chalcogenide growth. Its conversion can differ from that of other phosphine chalcogenides, changing how the composition and shape evolve when several feeds compete.

statements.title: Tributylphosphine as a chalcogen carrier
statements.summary: Tributylphosphine can react with elemental chalcogen to form a soluble molecular phosphine chalcogenide feed. When that feed supplies growing nanocrystals, its conversion rate affects the availability of chalcogen for nucleation and growth.

statements.title: Hydrated sulfide as an aqueous feed
statements.summary: Hydrated sodium sulfide dissolves to supply sulfide species for precipitation of metal sulfide nanocrystals. The acidity and metal complexation determine how quickly those species become available for nucleation.

statements.title: Washing ligand-coated iodide perovskite dots
statements.summary: When methyl acetate is used as an antisolvent, it helps separate hydrophobic cesium lead iodide dots from soluble residues. Washing must balance cleanup against loss of weakly bound surface ligands needed for stable dispersions.

statements.title: Silica growth by alkoxide condensation
statements.summary: In alcohol-based silica sol-gel synthesis, tetraethoxysilane hydrolyzes and the resulting species condense into a silica network. The balance between hydrolysis, nucleation and further condensation influences the particle-size distribution.

statements.title: Silica growth by alkoxide condensation
statements.summary: In alcohol-based silica sol-gel synthesis, tetraethyl orthosilicate hydrolyzes and the resulting species condense into a silica network. The balance between hydrolysis, nucleation and further condensation influences the particle-size distribution.

statements.title: Dispersing iron oxide after precipitation
statements.summary: When used to peptize washed iron oxide particles, tetramethylammonium hydroxide provides an alkaline environment that favors a charged oxide surface. Electrostatic repulsion can stabilize an aqueous ferrofluid without growth of a new solid phase.

statements.title: Dispersing ligand-exchanged lead sulfide dots
statements.summary: In solution processing of lead sulfide dots, dimethylformamide can disperse particles after their native long-chain ligands are exchanged for ionic surface ligands. Changing that surface shell can change dot spacing and electronic coupling after the solvent is removed.

statements.title: A solvated tellurium feed for chalcogenide growth
statements.summary: Trioctylphosphine telluride allows tellurium to be supplied in a soluble phosphine-bound form. When tellurium conversion competes with other chalcogen sources, their different delivery rates can influence which material forms at each growth stage.

statements.title: A silyl selenium precursor reacts differently from a phosphine feed
statements.summary: Bis(trimethylsilyl)selenide is a reactive selenium source for nonaqueous metal selenide growth. Controlling its delivery helps control whether the available selenium is consumed by new nuclei or incorporated into existing nanocrystals.

statements.title: Silyl arsine conversion makes delivery important
statements.summary: Tris(trimethylsilyl)arsine can react rapidly with an indium precursor to form indium arsenide. The rate at which the feeds meet and become available together can affect the balance between fresh nuclei and growth of existing dots.

statements.title: Lead chloride and sulfur supply distinct growth species in oleylamine
statements.summary: When colloidal lead sulfide is grown from a lead halide and sulfur in oleylamine, the amine environment affects sulfur activation and coordination of the soluble metal feed. Their relative availability can affect particle growth and the nature of the resulting surface.

statements.title: A thiol can both supply sulfur and bind the surface
statements.summary: In metal-sulfide routes that use an alkanethiol as the sulfur feed, metal–thiolate chemistry can supply sulfur to the growing lattice. Thiol or thiolate species can also bind at the particle surface, so sulfur delivery and surface capping may be linked.

statements.title: Elemental sulfur can be delivered in a noncoordinating liquid
statements.summary: When dissolved in octadecene for cadmium sulfide growth, elemental sulfur can supply the chalcogen without first being prepared as a phosphine sulfide. Its activation competes with metal precursor conversion and helps determine when the crystalline phase begins to form.

statements.title: A phosphine-free selenium feed has different chemistry
statements.summary: When used as a phosphine-free feed in non-injection cadmium selenide synthesis, selenium dispersed or dissolved in octadecene has different conversion chemistry from phosphine-bound selenium. The choice of reaction medium changes the supply of growth species and can shift the balance between discrete clusters and continued growth.

statements.title: Arsenic supply sets the growth surface environment
statements.summary: The group-V to group-III supply ratio helps determine how arsenic-rich the surface remains during indium arsenide growth. Changing arsenic pressure at a fixed indium supply can alter surface incorporation and the way strained islands grow.

statements.title: Isopropanol can help recover ligand-capped particles
statements.summary: In a hot-injection workup, isopropanol can act as an antisolvent for nanocrystals capped with long-chain ligands. Which particles precipitate depends on how well the solvent mixture keeps their ligand shells dispersed, so the wash can select the recovered fraction without changing the growth reaction.

statements.title: Preparing a selenium feed in phosphine
statements.summary: Elemental selenium powder can be dissolved in trioctylphosphine to prepare a soluble feed for cadmium selenide hot injection. Preparing the stock first separates selenium dissolution from the injection that starts nanocrystal nucleation.

fallback.title: Thermodynamics and kinetics
fallback.summary: Thermodynamics describes which states are energetically favoured, while kinetics governs how quickly a system can move between them. A change can be favourable yet proceed slowly when an activation barrier or limited transport restricts the pathway.
